d.d: Used to form the "anterior future", or "future in the past", indicating a futurity relative to a past time.
d.x: On my first day at University, I met the woman who would become my wife.

d.d: Used to, did repeatedly, habitually; indicates an action that happened several times in the past (cannot describe continuous states, as in I used to live in London)
Was or were determined to; indicating someone's insistence upon doing something.
Something that would happen, or would be the case, under different circumstances; a potentiality.
would not (negative auxiliary)
d.x: Wouldn't you often have supper on the terrace on Sundays?

d.d: An injury, such as a cut, stab, or tear, to a (usually external) part of the body.
An injury to a person by which the skin is divided or its continuity broken.

d.x: It took a long time to get over the wound of that insult.

d.d: To hurt or injure (someone) by cutting, piercing, or tearing the skin.
d.x: The police officer wounded the suspect during the fight that ensued.

d.d: To hurt (a person's feelings).
d.x: The actor's pride was wounded when the leading role went to his rival.
